reference.title: Janda Sit up
reference.listing: GymVisual page could not be read (gymvisual.com blocked by the proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching knowledge

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl up slowly, inhale as you roll back down.
breathing.cadence: About 2 s up, a short pause, 2 s down

prescription.tempo: Slow: about 2 s up, 1 s pause, 2 s down
prescription.progression: Slower reps and a longer pause; arms crossed on the chest, then hands by the ears

cues.text: Lie on your back, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat and free (not anchored). Arms straight, reaching toward the knees.
Press the heels down into the mat and pull them gently toward you (hamstrings on) as you breathe out and curl the head and shoulders up.
Keep curling slowly until the trunk is roughly halfway up; heels stay pressed down and the feet stay on the mat.
Roll back down slowly, one vertebra at a time, heels still pressing.
Rest briefly with the head down; repeat without momentum.

mistakes.fix: Keep pressing the heels down and pulling back; curl only as far as the feet stay down.
Arms just reach; the abdominals do the work slowly.
The feet stay free: that is the point of the Janda version.

kinematics.measure: Trunk (pelvis to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: Roughly halfway up: the hip flexors are meant to be quiet, so the sit-up stays mostly trunk flexion (clinical opinion)
Less than in a full sit-up (clinical opinion; full sit-ups add hip flexion in the second half, Andersson 1997)
About 90 degrees, heels pressed down and back (clinical opinion)
Slow, about 2 s up and 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #22554, Janda Sit up, video (movement reference; page not readable here)

Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
The idea that a hamstring press silences the hip flexors is a clinical claim; it is not well supported by EMG data (clinical opinion).
Low-back pain or flexion intolerance: curl-ups load the spine less than sit-ups (Axler and McGill 1997; McGill 1998).
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest and keep the chin slightly tucked.
Hamstring cramps: press the heels more gently.
regressions: Curl-up with the arms reaching to the knees.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the trunk slowly against gravity; free feet mean the abdominals cannot lean on the hip flexors as much as in an anchored sit-up (Andersson 1997 found anchoring raised hip-flexor activity).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: Heels press down and pull back so the hamstrings co-contract (the intended Janda cue; clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hamstrings_l: Heels press down and pull back so the hamstrings co-contract (the intended Janda cue; clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Intended to stay quiet; measured hip-flexor activity in Janda-style sit-ups is debated (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Intended to stay quiet; measured hip-flexor activity in Janda-style sit-ups is debated (clinical opinion).
